text: After the death of Saul, when David had returned from defeating the Amalekites, he stayed in Ziklag two days.
On the third day a man came from Saul's camp, his clothes torn and dirt on his head. When he came to David, he fell to the ground and bowed low.
David asked him, "Where have you come from?" He answered, "I escaped from the camp of Israel."
"Tell me what happened," David said. He replied, "The army fled from the battle. Many of the men fell and died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too."
Then David said to the young man who brought the report, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?"
The young man said, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, with the chariots and horsemen closing in on him.
He turned around and saw me, and he called out to me. I said, 'Here I am.'
He asked me, 'Who are you?' I answered, 'I am an Amalekite.'
Then he said to me, 'Stand over me and kill me. The agony has gripped me, but I am still alive.'

versions.text: Then he said to me, 'Come here and kill me. The agony has gripped me, but I am still alive.'
versions.explanation: The Hebrew עֲמָד־נָא עָלַי means "stand over me," and the same idiom is deliberately echoed in verse 10 ("So I stood over him"). Rendering it "Come here" breaks that verbal link and slightly weakens the narrative parallel; "Stand over me" is both accurate and reads well aloud.

text: So I stood over him and killed him, for I knew he could not survive after he had fallen. Then I took the crown from his head and the band from his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."
Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men with him.
They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and his son Jonathan, for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
David said to the young man who had brought him the report, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite."
David said to him, "How is it you were not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?"
Then David called one of his men and said, "Go, strike him down!" So he struck him, and he died.
For David had said to him, "Your blood is on your own head, for your own mouth testified against you when you said, 'I killed the LORD's anointed.'"
Then David sang this lament for Saul and his son Jonathan,
and he ordered that the people of Judah be taught this song, called The Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar:

versions.text: and he ordered that the people of Judah be taught this Song of the Bow. It is written in the Book of Jashar:
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads simply "to teach the sons of Judah the bow"; the word "Song" is supplied by interpretation. Making the title explicit as "called The Bow" keeps the added words visible to the listener while preserving the natural flow. A footnote could note: "Hebrew simply 'the bow,' probably the title of the lament."

text: Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen!
Tell it not in Gath, proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, or the daughters of the Philistines will rejoice, the daughters of the uncircumcised will exult.
Mountains of Gilboa, may you have no dew or rain, nor fields that yield offerings. For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, no longer anointed with oil.
From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not turn back, the sword of Saul did not return empty.

versions.text: From the blood of the slain, from the flesh of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan did not turn back, the sword of Saul did not return empty.
versions.explanation: חֵלֶב means "fat," not "flesh" (בָּשָׂר). The poetic pairing "blood ... fat" is a deliberate image of the weapons being sated in battle; "flesh" flattens the metaphor and is lexically inaccurate.

text: Saul and Jonathan—beloved and gracious in life, in death they were not parted. They were swifter than eagles, stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul, who clothed you in scarlet and finery, who adorned your garments with gold.
How the mighty have fallen in the midst of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights.
I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were very dear to me. Your love for me was wonderful, surpassing the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!
